title: Module 2 · Enabling Organizational Strategy through Information Systems
description: Interactive module on using information systems strategically: decision-making levels, automating versus organizational learning versus strategy, Porter's five competitive forces, value chain analysis, business and revenue models, platforms and network effects, innovation, where AI belongs in strategy work, runnable spreadsheet and SQL exercises, and a rehearsal of the whole strategy analysis as one deliverable.
hero:
Module 2

Enabling Organizational Strategy through Information Systems

Module 1 asked what an information system is. This one asks the harder question a manager actually gets paid to answer: which system, where, and why that one. A company can spend heavily on technology and end up merely faster at what it already did. The difference between spending and strategy is a way of thinking — about where the pressure in your industry comes from, where in your own operation value is created, and what a competitor would have to do to copy you.

How to use this page

  1. Read the short setup first. Every term is explained in ordinary language before an activity uses it, so nothing assumes a background you have not been given.
  2. Answer as you go. The activities sit inside the reading. When you answer a question, every option explains itself — including the three you did not pick, because knowing why a wrong answer is wrong is the part that transfers.
  3. Write real formulas and real queries. The last section is not a description of a spreadsheet and a database. You type into them and they run, on the page, against real rows — and they tell you plainly when something will not work.
  4. Retry anything. Restart one activity, one section, or the whole page. Your best result stays in this browser until you clear it; answers reset on reload so every attempt is fresh.
  5. Finish with the final challenge. Thirty-nine situations, scored by objective, so a weak area shows up instead of being averaged away.

Where this module sits in the course objectives

The three modules are organized around the textbook’s own learning objectives, but the course is graded against a different list. This table says plainly which of the eleven course objectives this module serves, and which ones it does not, so you always know why you are reading something.

Course objectiveWhat this module does with it
3. Discuss how companies use information technology for competitive advantage by changing their marketplace This module’s main job. Where to compete and how to compete supply the two analyses, competitive forces and the value chain. Business models in the digital world and revenue, platforms and network effects show the marketplace itself being rearranged rather than merely entered. The two innovation sections cover holding an advantage once it has been won, and the closing supplement runs the whole analysis end to end on a single firm.
2. Discuss how companies use information systems to manage internal operations and to make decisions Also central. Decision levels and functional areas sorts decisions into operational, managerial and executive, separates the structured from the unstructured, and names the systems each functional area runs. Automate, learn, strategize then shows one ordinary process being asked to do three progressively harder things.
7. Recognize a business problem which might be solved using information technology, then work with the information systems team on a solution The first half, thoroughly. Naming the pressure before naming the technology, telling a vague ask from a fundable one, running the method in the order the work is actually done, and pulling the evidence yourself before recommending anything. The closing supplement then runs all four moves as one connected piece of work, from the pressures a firm faces through to a written comparison of a set length. Developing and rolling out the system is still not covered.
5. Delineate how businesses use internet technology for electronic commerce, communicating with employees and working with business partners Supporting. The five-forces section traces what the internet did to each competitive pressure in turn; the value chain section covers exchanging orders, invoices and receipts with partners electronically; and the platforms section covers businesses that could not exist without it at all. The technology underneath is Module 3.
4. Apply a working knowledge of computer hardware, software, database technology and computer networks The database quarter. The analyst’s toolkit and strategy as code put real tables in front of you and have you ask them business questions, joining and grouping until the answer appears. Hardware, software and computer networks are Module 3’s.
8. Describe the individual and organizational consequences of the use of information technology Supporting. The platforms section takes the human side of that kind of work seriously rather than treating it as a footnote, and the artificial-intelligence supplement asks what should be handed to a machine and what a person has to keep. Module 1 carries the fuller treatment.
1. Describe what a company’s information systems department does · 6. Outline the life cycle of an information system · 9. Recognize security breaches and computer crimes Not taught here. What the information systems department does, and what a security breach looks like, are Module 1’s; the life cycle of a system is not covered in this module either.
10. Solve a business problem by creating a database application using SQLite · 11. Use advanced spreadsheet functions to create a decision support system Served by the course’s separate database and spreadsheet work. The analyst’s toolkit here rehearses the querying and text-cleaning skills that work builds on, without standing in for it.
Level

Who decides what

Operational, managerial and executive work need different systems because they face different kinds of decision.

Ambition

Faster, better, smarter

Three different reasons to build something, with three different payoffs — and only one of them is strategy.

Position

Where and how to compete

The five forces say what is squeezing you; the value chain says where you could answer it.

Evidence

Getting the numbers

A claim without evidence is a preference. Two tools close most of the gap between question and answer.

One idea connects the whole module Technology that everyone can buy cannot, by itself, make you different from everyone who bought it. Advantage comes from what you put around the technology — the processes, the data and the people — which is why this module spends its time on analysis rather than on products.

Chapter vocabulary

Every term the chapter defines, in one place, written so it makes sense on its own. Search by word, or filter by the objective the term belongs to. Use this while you read rather than after — a good deal of the difficulty in this chapter is two terms that sound alike meaning genuinely different things, such as efficiency and effectiveness, or a resource and a capability.
finalIntro:
Put it together

Final challenge

Thirty-nine situations rather than thirty-nine definitions. Each describes something happening in an organization and asks what is actually going on, which is the form this material takes once you are the person being asked. Answer all of them, then score: the result breaks out by objective, so a weak area points at the section to reread instead of disappearing into a single number.
foot: What to do next. Take one organization you already deal with and run the whole chain on it once: name the force that squeezes it hardest, find the value chain activity where that force lands, say what system would relieve it, and state the number that should move. Then ask what evidence would settle whether you are right, and how you would pull it. That last question is the one that separates an opinion from an analysis.
